speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I gladly subscribe to the expressions of congratulation which have been extended by most of the hon. members who have preceded me to those two honourable and gallant members of this house, to use the phraseology of Westminster, who were chosen by the government to move and second the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. When they made their speeches they wore the king's uniform, and I think it is true that in choosing those two hon. members for the task the government paid a tribute to the fighting services of which they are
members, and also did honour to the two hon. members themselves. I listened with unusual attention to what they said, because it appears to me that such men must of necessity have their sayings brightened by the breadth of their experience, they having offered themselves in this struggle on our behalf; and I feel sure that the whole house will wish them great success in what lies ahead.
Since the house last met, the party to which I belong has held a most important convention. It received the resignation of a leader; it chose his successor; it added a word to the name of the party, and it brought the policy of the party up to date in conformity with the trend of public opinion throughout the world. It is not unusual that the Conservative party should thus review its policy from time to time, because a study of history will, I think, show all people with open minds that in the past it has been the Conservative party that has marched along the road of progress in this country. In choosing our new leader we have selected a man who has not been closely associated in the past with any political party. He is a man of vision, a man not given to phraseology or to evasion. What he says he means; what he means he says, and I believe he is understood by the common people. Perhaps he subscribes to the view which I have held for a considerable time with regard to partisanship. Under our democratic system of government a political party is a most valuable instrument, and as long as it is used as an instrument and kept in the position of a servant it is not only useful but almost a necessity in our form of government. But it must never become the master, for if it does it has a sway which is so dominating that it has an evil effect upon the policies adopted by the party. It will not be at all difficult for me to give allegiance to our new leader, and I note with considerable interest the acclaim with which his choice has been received throughout Canada among those who subscribe to the party to which I belong.
The amendment which we of the official opposition have drawn to the attention of the house is threefold. It deals with man-power, with the policy in regard to labour, and with agriculture. We maintain that criticism is due the government on account of the lack of success attending their efforts in these three directions. Labour is the thread that runs . through all three, and we certainly have not arrived at that degree of success which we had anticipated after the national selective service scheme was put into operation. There is in this country a given quantity of labour available for the many purposes to which it must
The Address-Mr. Stirling

be put. But under national selective service labour has not found its way under proper allocation into these various channels. In the part of British Columbia from which I come the principal interest is agriculture in its most varied forms, and there is also mining. Along with both these industries, however, are the various secondary industries which attach themselves to any main industry; and in all these walks of life we have been looking on during a period of considerable difficulty as a result of lack of labour. It is common to all parts of Canada. It is a difficulty which must be foreseen and which has been foreseen, and it is a difficulty which must be met. In the first place it must be met by the ingenuity of those who are concerned in the industries using that labour, but over and above that, after they have used all the ingenuity within their power, there must be direction at the top or there will be failure.
With regard to matters other than the particular industries involved in this question, I should imagine that right across Canada, and certainly in British Columbia, a very grave difficulty exists at the present time in connection with the matter of fuel. The supply of coal has been intermittent. Coal, however, is not the principal fuel used by those whom I represent. They use wood in various forms, whether in cord-wood or in sawdust; and because during the past year or two those who customarily put in their winter cutting wood and storing it for future use have not been available for this work, such stores of fuel have become used up. Unfortunately, during the bitter weather we had recently, our people had to warm themselves and to cook with green lumber; and hon. members who have attempted to cook with green lumber will know the difficulties which have been experienced in almost every home in British Columbia. The situation is bad enough in the rural areas, but in the cities it has reached the point of endangering life. I do not suggest that this is a matter with regard to which the dominion government can just step in and provide a remedy, but what I do suggest is that the fuel administrator must go far more deeply into this question of the people's fuel in order that plans may be evolved which will overcome the difficulty; for we must not forget that if we have completely run out of dry fuel, next winter must be planned for long before next winter arrives.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house two matters, both either directly or indirectly concerning labour. In the south of the constituency of Yale and along the United States border is the country in which Douk-

hobors live, and they run over into the neighbouring riding of Kootenay West. As this house well knows, they have been a constant source of difficulty to governments in Canada. When the registration measure of 1940 was instituted, Doukhobors, of course, were subservient to it, as were all of us. Some of the Doukhobors filled in the necessary forms, while others did not. Those who did not were not permitted, under the terms of the registration, to hire themselves out for work, nor might anyone employ such unregistered persons. Throughout that southern country, however, where a great deal of lumbering is carried on, and where the contracts undertaken by the lumber operators have largely been government orders, there has been a considerable shortage of labour. There has been a tendency for the lumber mills to employ unregistered Doukhobors. This applies not only to the lumber mills, but to other industries including the section gangs of the transportation companies.
Obviously the law has not been enforced with regard to these unregistered Doukhobors, with the natural consequence that Canadian residents in those parts look upon this as unfair treatment of them and their sons. As a result of the registration their sons are called up; they go to training camps and carry out the duties of young Canadians. But the Doukhobors do not. Ever since their ancestors arrived in 1898, they have been treated differently. Although they have not been placed in training camps, they have not been used in any other work. This is resented all through the country in which the Doukhobors live.
Last summer I was speaking about the matter to a police officer, and he said, "Look at the position in which we are placed. If we go out and demand registration cards, taking action if they are not produced, we are informed by our senior officers that it would be advisable not to be too stiff. If we do not take action, then the public will say, 'You are not putting the Doukhobors under the penalties of the registration regulations, but you are bringing the same penalties to bear upon us and our sons'." Is it any wonder that strong resentment exists in that part of the country?
Late last summer I paid a visit to Grand Forks, and heard resentment expressed . wherever I went. I wrote the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) a letter describing what I had found and, on the basis of the statements of people I had met, I made the suggestion that the minister send an official of his department through that southern

The Address-Mr. Stirling
country to investigate on the minister's behalf, to hear what the inhabitants had to say, and to listen to any suggestions which responsible citizens who have been experiencing this trouble for a long time might make. I suggested that in that way the minister could inform himself at first hand from his official, and that a possible solution of the difficulty might be worked out. The minister was good enough to accept my suggestion and to say that such an official would be sent in. I wanted, not a commission, but rather a departmental official who could move around among the people, see conditions for himself, and listen to any suggestions.
We cannot go on year after year looking upon this Doukhobor question as something which cannot be solved. That would merely bring the law into disrepute. May I read two or three paragraphs from my letter to the minister:
Young Canadians by their age classes go to camp for military training and subsequent service. The Doukhobors do not. Is it any wonder that the inhabitants are angry or that the Doukhobors are laughing at us? Over the years my hope has been that time would solve the difficulty. I am sorry to say that the people in Grand Forks now tell me that the younger Doukhobors, with minds somewhat expanded, are taking the view that it is quite unnecessary to submit to regulation, because the government does not know what to do with them, and so it will continue to do nothing.
Then I made reference to the suggestion I have already outlined, namely, that an official be sent in to make inquiries on the spot. I concluded with this paragraph:
I am well aware that labour is short, that Doukhobors are employed, and that if they were discharged badly wanted produce would suffer. But the effect on the inhabitants of winking at breaches of the law by a Doukhobor, a law which is enforced on others, is very bad indeed.
A lumber operator said to me, "I must not employ unregistered Doukhobors; but if I see that my competitors are doing so, and if the section gangs on the railways use these men, what am I to do? I also have government contracts to fill." What he wanted, and what I request, is that the law be enforced on one as well as on the other; otherwise this Doukhobor question will go on, and become worse and worse.
The other question to which I should like to refer has to do with the Japanese. After the treachery of Japan, which precipitated us into war with that country, the anxiety on the Pacific coast and the danger of the situation induced the government to proclaim a protected area of varying width from the United States boundary to Alaska. The boundary of this area almost touches the southwest 72537-25
corner of the constituency of Yale which I have the honour to represent. We are therefore not in the protected area.
After the protected area had been so proclaimed, and after the government had intimated its policy of evacuating the Japanese from within that area, some of the Japanese did not wait to be evacuated, but trekked by day and night, by train and by car and, as soon as they crossed the line of delimitation, began to settle. My constituency was the first and possibly the most desirable piece of country in which they could settle, and as a result many of them stopped there.
Before this difficulty we had from 800 to 1,000 Japanese men, women and children who had been resident in. that area. I must say for them that they were good citizens and subscribed to the law. There was seldom any trouble from them, and they certainly worked. The houses and shacks of those inhabitants became the settling point of the Japanese trekking from the protected area. The result was that we saw many more oriental faces on the streets, in the stores, on the roads and in cars. They were not wanted immigrants. When the British Columbia security commission was first set up it appeared to be more interested in the evacuation of the Japanese from the protected area than in their destination. Strong protestations were made by those living to the east of that protected area that those Japanese must not be allowed to squat among them. Eventually the commission instituted a permit system, and without a permit a Japanese could not move from the protected area.
A committee was set up to cover the interior from Kamloops to the boundary, 200 miles away, whose purpose it was to reflect public opinion on this matter and deal with the security commission. The representations of the committee were not always received with evident pleasure by the commission, but they were received and in some instances they were * acted upon. When the labour difficulties of last year arose, when the thinning of the fruit, the weeding of vegetables and the eventual harvesting and picking were upon us, it was found to be extremely hard to save that valuable crop. But the inhabitants of the interior, both the farmers and the townfolk, worked admirably together, and there is nothing but praise to be said of those business men of the towns who closed their stores for one or two days a week in order that those working in the stores could go out and help the farmers with their harvest.
There were other districts, principally toward the northern end of the fruit and vegetable

The Address-Mr. Stirling

belt, where such help was not available, and despite the use of high school students and any labour that could be induced to come in from outside, there was an obvious shortage in prospect. Some of the larger growers appealed to the security commission to bring in Japanese for labour, but the commission took the view that they would not agree to do that unless the municipalities concerned would give their consent. Eventually the security committee, not the commission, voicing the opinion of the public from Kamloops to the line, arrived at this formula. A grower desiring Japanese labour would be permitted to receive at his own expense that labour if it came in under police supervision, if it remained under police supervision, if it was to be returned to the place whence it came and if it was male only. The commission agreed to a certain extent to allow the fruit growers of some areas to receive such help. When it arrived, some of it was sent back immediately because it did not prove amenable, it was damaging the fruit by throwing it about and did not show any desire to work honestly. But those who remained were of great assistance in harvesting the crop.
However, only certain fruit growers in certain areas were ready to adopt this means of saving their crop. Away to the south, and dotted through the whole area, were those who would not agree on any terms whatever to more Japanese being brought into the district. Why was that? I feel certain it was because these people had a longer vision. They saw that if Japanese came into that area and settled, the tendency would be for more and more to come in; they had not forgotten the experience of people in other parts of the world, especially in the fruit valleys of California and, to a lesser extent, in the lower mainland of our own province of British Columbia, and they would not consent to these people coming in.
I would remind the house that for many years there has been a provincial government prohibition of the use of orientals in logging from crown lands as well as in connection with government contracts taken by sawmill operators. Why did the provincial government take that line, and why have they maintained it? I think it is because they had a longer vision of the result of scattering Japanese and other orientals through the interior country. Recently the dominion government approached the provincial government at Victoria to ascertain whether they would remove that prohibition because of the war and allow Japanese labour to be used in logging camps. The provincial government has declined to remove the prohibition, although it recognizes that under the
'Mr. Stirling.]
War Measures Act the dominion government could, if it chose, override this prohibition. Even with the difficulty of obtaining labour the provincial government has not seen fit to raise this prohibition.
The commission's task was not an easy one because they had to find destinations and, as far as possible, occupations for some 24,000 Japanese. These Japanese were distributed through the interior of British Columbia in road camps and other places and, besides that, agreements were entered into with Alberta, Manitoba and Ontario to receive a certain number for work of specified description. I think 2,500 went to Alberta, 1,000 to Manitoba and some 500 to Ontario. These were moved under provincial government agreements, and in addition there were smaller numbers who went to particular industries in the other provinces. I would direct the attention of the house to the fact that each of these provincial agreements contained a clause under which the dominion government must arrange to remove these Japanese from these provinces after the war, should that desire be expressed. From the utterances of the public men of Canada I have no doubt whatever that that desire will be so ' expressed. Therefore the dominion government will be under contract to remove these Japanese.
The question that many people in British Columbia are asking themselves to-day is: To what place will these Japanese be removed? It must be remembered that the fishing boats of the Japanese who used to fish on the Pacific coast have been sold by the custodian of enemy property. It must also be remembered that business premises of Japanese firms which were located in the cities on the coast and in the rural parts of the province are being disposed of. I do not think it will be thought for a moment by anyone who knows anything about the feeling of the British Columbia people on this oriental question that Japanese will be received in any part of British Columbia with anything like equanimity.
I ask the government if it does not see fit to proclaim a policy in regard to this matter and allay public opinion. I emphasize the fact that this oriental question has been debated in this house year after year for a quarter of a century. Twenty years ago it was an annual event. British Columbia considered that this was a question of greater magnitude than a provincial matter, and I was shocked last year when a minister of this government referred to it as a provincial question, as a British Columbia question, and made the statement that we in the original years of their intrusion asked them to come.

The Address-Mr. Ross (Calgary)
The opinion was faulty and the statement of fact was inaccurate. We never asked them to come. Forty years ago or thereabouts the Japanese government removed the prohibition which had existed until then upon emigration. In those days the Japanese might not leave Japan, but the Japanese government removed that prohibition. From then on. the Japanese started to come into British Columbia in, a trickle which grew into a stream. They came, but we never asked them. Although to-day we employ some of them as labour and some find their vocation in contracts with farmers for garden truck, the great majority of them are not working for wages but have set themselves up in business premises or on farms where they are their own masters. I raise this question in this house for this definite purpose, that British Columbia considers that it has long enough been allowed to carry this burden alone. The conditions of entanglement which existed in the earlier years of this century on account of the Anglo-Japanese alliance have now ended. The treachery of the Japanese has shown to us that we cannot look behind that oriental face and realize with any certainty where their patriotism lies. Have they given up their patriotism? Have they given up their original nationality? We do not know; we shall never know.
I draw further attention to this fact, that the many who have been born in Canada, and who in accordance with our law may be described as Canadian subjects, have in many instances been the more cnfficult to work with and to handle under these circumstances than have been the nationals. The really bad actors were interned immediately, but many of those men of whom nothing evil was known have been placed in camps or have been sent out under the schemes to which I have referred or have found occupation of some sort. The matter has been handled and is settled perhaps for the present. But it is the future we are thinking of, and I ask the government if it will not see fit to proclaim its policy with regard to the future, because I warn the government that if after this war comes to an end these people are allowed to -roam in British Columbia there will be trouble enough for the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to take part in this debate until I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) announce a few days ago that the budget would be brought down in the course of two or three weeks. It then occurred to me that if any member had any injustices or grievances which he wished to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance, it would 72537-251
be an opportune time to do so while he is considering his budget.
There are two matters in particular which I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. One is the excessive taxes which are imposed under the Income War Tax Act upon commissioned officers while they remain in Canada. I conceive it to be the duty of a member of this house to inform himself of any injustices under which the active forces may be labouring and to do what he can to adjust them. I suggest that for this reason. The forces have a right to complain to their commanding officers of any injustice, but they have no right, as they understand the situation, to complain to a member of this house. Their commanding officers cannot do anything toward redressing the grievance of which I am speaking, and for that reason I think it is our duty to be on the alert to bring grievances of this kind to the attention of the house.
Prior to 1940 all soldiers were taxed on their income and allowances, but in 1940 the act was amended to exempt non-commissioned officers and all other ranks in all forces from the income tax. Commissioned officers were also exempted as long as they were serving overseas, but commissioned officers serving in Canada were required under the act as then amended to pay full income tax. At the last session of the house I directed the attention of the minister and of the house to this matter because I thought it worked an injustice particularly on the lower paid officers. I pointed out at that time that these commissioned officers volunteered for service anywhere in the world, that they were ready, willing and anxious, indeed preferred, to go overseas, and yet they were heavily taxed simply because they were kept in Canada. The minister at that time promised to do something for these men. He did something for them, a little, not very much. I submit that he should have done a great deal more, and I hope that now something more will be done in this respect.
Let us consider the circumstances. A warrant officer, class 1, grade A, is not taxed. His income is $150.56 a month. The net income of a captain, a higher officer, while he is serving in Canada is only S133.67. The net income of a lieutenant is $108.58; of a second lieutenant, S96.97. A warrant officer, lower in rank than a second lieutenant, nevertheless draws $53.59 more pay after taxation is deducted, and he draws $41.98 a month more than a lieutenant, $16.89 more than a captain, and within $3.46 of the pay of a major. A staff-sergeant also receives more than a lieutenant after the tax has been deducted from the latter's pay. I am not suggesting that the

The Address-Mr. Ross (Calgary)
warrant officer or the staff-sergeant is paid too much. They are not paid too much, nor do I quarrel with the pay that is being given to a lieutenant, a second lieutenant, a captain or a major. What I do object to is that the government is paying these higher ranks more pay with one hand and then taking it away in taxes with the other. We boast that our army is the best paid, the best clothed, the best housed and the best fed army in the world. But what is the advantage in paying these commissioned officers well while they are in Canada if we take a large part of it away in taxes? The commissioned officers are taxed so highly that there is no inducement for a noncommissioned officer to seek promotion. There is no inducement for a man to rise from the ranks to the position of commissioned officer. That should not be the situation. As it is now, if he is promoted he must live on so much less.
There are other perquisites given to noncommissioned officers and others in the ranks to which the commissioned officer is not entitled. The commissioned officer must pay for his own clothing and equipment, except that when he is appointed to a commission he is allowed $150 with which to buy clothing and equipment. But it takes another $150 to $250 from his own pocket in order to buy all the necessary equipment, and he must also pay $75 to $100 a year for replacements, and another $75 a year or thereabouts for extra messing costs. These outgoings are in addition to what a non-commissioned officer or a private is required to pay.
But that is not all. The dependent's board of trustees provide special assistance to dependents of men serving in the Canadian navy, army or air force. I quote from their circular, August, 1942:
What kind of assistance?
Financial-over and above what is already received under the existing marriage or dependents' allowance regulations. . . .
Who are eligible for financial assistance?
Dependents of members of the Canadian armed forces below the rank of warrant officer class I who are in receipt of marriage or dependents' allowance and who are in special or urgent need.
These concessions do not inure to the benefit of commissioned officers.
So far I have discussed only the position of the single man with no dependents. A married man is in a much worse position. A considerable portion of his pay must 'be assigned to his wife and family for their maintenance and support. As long as he is
[Mr! G. H. Rosa.]
living in Canada he likes to have a home near where he is stationed, so that he may occasionally visit his wife and family. If he is about to be sent overseas he likes to get home during his embarkation leave, and if his family are not located near him it is very difficult for him, on his small pay, to raise the necessary money. In 1940 railway rates were such that a soldier returning home on leave could make the return trip for single fare. I regarded the charge as excessive, and on November 7, 1940, I brought the matter to the attention of the minister and of this house, and urged that concessions in the way of railway rates should be made to men in the armed forces while on leave, particularly embarkation leave. A good deal has been done in that respect, but even with the small rates which are exacted to-day it is very difficult for a commissioned officer stationed, say, at Halifax to return to Calgary on embarkation leave; the pay is so meagre that he can scarcely afford to do it.
There is another matter to which I wish to refer. When he is discharged from the army he receives a cheque for a month's pay. That is all very well, but at the same time he is told that he owes the government eight months' arrears of income tax. That is not a happy prospect for the commissioned officer. The private has no such obligation. It is not just that the officer should be subject to this requirement, and I suggest that it is a condition which should be remedied.
Furthermore, a commissioned officer is held responsible for all equipment and supplies entrusted to his command. The private has no such worries.
I hope the minister will give this matter careful consideration and do something to relieve the situation.
On motion of Mr. Ross (Calgary East) the debate was adjourned.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the
house adjourned at six p.m.
